problem: What linear transformation $T$ is represented by the matrix $T=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]?$

activity_context.topic_title: Dilations and Reflections as Linear Transformations

examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Linear Transformation Represented by a Matrix
examples.problem:
What linear transformation is represented by the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/0394b5d3a371caf95d5e701c0ffb00894eb685e706d8b70af2149057de0b0cb5.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as depicted below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14060608/assets/b93bb91dae85a3e3b40a8d0ade3d4f420064aaa6926431fa7f664c977bb8fd59.png)

Therefore, the matrix represents the reflection across the $x$-axis.

feedback.problem: A linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation.  Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}-60 \\ -9\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ -3\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-60 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=\frac{1}{3}v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=\frac{1}{3}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$
